End of Round and Scoring 3 Options 3.1 Number of Rounds 3.2 Pass Rule 3.3 No Trump Bid 3.4 Adjutant Selection Timing 3.5 Left Jack vs Same Two 3.6 Joker Strength on Lead 3.7 Joker Strength on Follow 3.8 Club 3 Joker Request 3.9 Perfect 20 Loses 4 References What is Napoleon? Napoleon is a trick-taking card game widely played in Japan. It uses a standard 53-card deck (including one Joker) and is played with 4–5 players (most often 5). Each round, the player who wins the bidding becomes "Napoleon" and secretly teams up with an "Adjutant" to try to capture at least as many picture cards (10, J, Q, K, A) as they declared. The other players form the "Allies" and try to stop them. Who the Adjutant is will be revealed during play, so guessing who is on your team and who is against you is a key of the game. How to Play Each round goes through the following steps. 1. Deal All 53 cards are dealt. 5 players: 10 cards each, with 3 cards left in the stock. 4 players: 12 cards each, with 5 cards left in the stock. 2. Bidding Players take turns declaring the number of picture cards they believe Napoleon's team (Napoleon and the Adjutant) can capture, along with a trump suit. Each bid must be stronger than the one before it. If you do not want to bid, you can pass. On BGA, the minimum bid is 8. The maximum is 20 (all picture cards). Bid strength is decided first by the number — a higher number is always stronger. If the numbers are the same, the suit decides, in this order * : ♠ > ♥ > ♦ > ♣ For example, " ♦ 10" is stronger than "♣ 10", and "♠ 12" is stronger than " ♦ 12". Any suit at 13 is stronger than any suit at 12. A player who has passed can bid again * . Bidding ends when all other players have passed. The last player still bidding becomes Napoleon for that round. If all players pass, the cards are redealt. 3. Adjutant Selection Napoleon chooses one card that is not in their hand and names it as the "Adjutant card" * . The player who holds that card becomes the secret Adjutant and joins Napoleon's team. Who the Adjutant is stays secret until the Adjutant card is played (except for the Adjutant themselves). If the chosen card is in the stock, Napoleon plays solo. 4. Card Exchange Napoleon takes the stock into their hand and then discards the same number of cards (5 players: 3 cards, 4 players: 5 cards). Discarded cards are removed from the game. Any picture cards among the discards count as captured by the Allies. 5. Trick-Taking Napoleon leads the first trick (plays the first card), and play goes clockwise, with each player playing one card. Basic Rules Lead : The lead player can play any card. The suit of that card becomes the "lead suit" for the trick. Follow suit : If you have a card of the lead suit, you must play it. If you have no card of the lead suit, you can play any card. Trick winner : The player who played the strongest card wins the trick and captures all picture cards from that trick. The winner leads the next trick. [Rating: 3/10] Trick taker, reminded me of Euchre without the funky Jacks and some strategy in exchanging cards/bidding.

[Rating: 4/10] Average trick taking game made a bit more interesting by the introduction of the secret partnership.  However as it takes six people to play you sacrifice a fair bit of the control that is usually present in other trick taking games.  Not being a fan of trick taking games generally I find this one every so slightly better than average due to the fun tensions involved in wondering who the secretary is in each hand.  --update-- Discovering Mu has knocked a point off of this one.

[Rating: 4/10] Used to play this game a lot. It is my first trick-taking game. Very popular in Japan.

[Rating: 5/10] [thing=23570][/thing] is a traditional card game about trick-taking and bidding. Players will bid on the number of face cards they will win (with 2p, the variant is bidding on the number of tricks). The winner of the bid picks the suit and name a card, and form a initially secret team with the person holding the named card. Points are awarded in several different ways, and after a number of rounds, the person(s) with the most points will be the winner. [Rating: 6/10] The secret partnerships are fun as is the bidding, but like most card games that aren't Tichu, I find myself bored after a while.  Bad hands are not fun and you just have to go thru the motions.  Good hands are fun, but you can normally tell if your gonna win or not.

[Rating: 7/10] Standard deck. Secret partnership. 5-6 player "picture game" from Japan. Fairly streamlined: bid for trump suit and how many tricks your team will win, Call a card for your (hidden) partner. The A spades is the "mighty" highest card bit still considered part of its suit. Neatest feature is that if all cards of same suit a 2 can beat everything but the Mighty and bowers.  Joker forces players to play trumps, and 3 clubs is a "joker killer". [Rating: 7/10] A simple bidding and trick taking game in which each player bids a number of tricks and then declarer attempts to win at least that many, with a chosen trump suit, from a 5-card hand. Nap is a largely forgotten card game these days, Euchre seems much better established, although this is arguably superior (in spite of the date on the BGG entry it's unlikely that this predates Euchre) as variable bidding is used.

[Rating: 7/10] I love the "Same Two" rule but, for the rest of the game, I prefer this game's Korean descendant, "Mighty".

[Rating: 7/10] Napoleon is a fairly standard trick taking game with two twists.  One, they name a super trump card and the owner becomes their secret partner and the winning bidder gets to exchange cards with the kitty.

[Rating: 7/10] It's a pretty fun trick taking game and probably my favorite of the genre. You do feel like you have power as Napoleon and it is fun to try to figure out who your ally is. It's also fun to be on the opposing side and get tricked into supporting Napoleon's ally.

[Rating: 7.5/10] Rating is for "Japanese Napoleon", a 5-player game closely related to this item.  A refreshingly easy-to-teach trick-taking game with bidding and variable/hidden partnerships.
